title: Clermont's Guru Indian Restaurant Marks 12 Years of Northern Indian Classics
excerpt: Master Chef Uday Kadam's family-run Clermont eatery celebrates a dozen years of tandoor-fired favorites — and expands next door with The Venue, a new event space and Sunday brunch.
body:
• Guru Indian Restaurant at 2400 S. Highway 27 in Clermont, Florida, is celebrating 12 years in business, the South Lake Tablet reports — a milestone for the family-run eatery founded in 2014 by Master Chef Uday Kadam.
  • The restaurant's honors include Best Restaurant, Best Fine Dining Restaurant and Best Indian Food Restaurant titles, eight straight years among TripAdvisor's top Central Florida picks, and a Top 10% Worldwide ranking on its 11th anniversary last November, according to the Daily Commercial.
  • Kadam's path ran from a village south of Mumbai — where his father was his first "Guru" — through the Taj Mahal Hotel in Bombay, Marriott kitchens in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, and Disney's Polynesian Resort, where he was food and beverage manager before opening Guru.
  • Planning a visit: The Venue, Kadam's new event space next door at 2400 S. U.S. 27, hosts a Sunday brunch every week from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. — $34.95 for adults, $19.95 for children under 12. Details at thevenueclermont.com or 352-227-3729.

The news

Twelve years after Master Chef Uday Kadam opened the doors of Guru Indian Restaurant in Clermont, the Lake County landmark is marking its dozen with food, festivity — and an expansion. The South Lake Tablet's anniversary feature, "Guru Indian Restaurant Celebrates 12 Tasty Years," also spotlights the restaurant's newest venture: The Venue, a multipurpose event space offering Clermont a dedicated home for weddings, galas and holiday parties.

For a suburban Indian restaurant to thrive for over a decade in Central Florida is no small feat. Guru has done it by becoming what Kadam calls his best work — "Out of 10, Guru is my best," he told Lake & Sumter Style.

The chef behind it

Kadam's story begins in a small village south of Mumbai, where he grew up watching his father cook. "My father was my first 'Guru,'" he recalls. Hired to cook at an airport canteen at 16, he later trained at Bombay's Taj Mahal Hotel, worked for Marriott in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, and came to the United States in 1982.

Florida became his stage: food and beverage manager at Disney's Polynesian Resort, then founder of Passage to India, a chain of eight restaurants on International Drive and across Orlando. Guru was the pivot to something personal. "Tourists go home," he says, "but at Guru, it's local people and those who have followed me through the years that we serve, and you develop relationships with them."

"In the olden days, restaurant owners were visible, but today many of them manage from the office. I still like to greet and talk to my customers as much as possible."

— Uday Kadam, owner and Master Chef, Guru Indian Restaurant

He started with two chefs and six employees; today the kitchen runs with eight cooks and 25 staff. The pandemic-era promotion — a free bottle of wine with pickup orders — proved so popular he kept it, and birthday diners still get a free entrée.

The food

Guru's menu tours northern Indian and biryani specialties, all made from scratch. Appetizers run from tandoori chicken and shrimp to lentil soup; entrées span masala, curry, vindaloo and Peshawari preparations of chicken, beef, lamb and seafood, with palak paneer among the vegetarian standouts. Breads come straight from the tandoor, and heat levels run mild to hot. Dessert means kulfi with pistachios, gulab jamun and rice pudding; Kadam's pick for the adventurous is the Peshawari naan, stuffed with almonds, dates, pistachio and golden raisins. "If people leave hungry, they will not come back," he says. "I make sure they get enough so they leave very satisfied or have leftovers to take home for later."

The diaspora angle

Guru is a case study in how Indian restaurateurs have become cultural anchors in American suburbs. Kadam's wife Pamela Carver designed the dining room — white linen tablecloths, a fresh rose on every table, traditional artwork and Indian melodies — to transport guests "to another world." "Sometimes people don't think they like Indian cooking until they try Guru," Kadam says. Beyond the dining room, he supports local police and fire departments, and on his 70th birthday hosted a free buffet for first responders and more than 3,000 boarding-school children in his Indian hometown.

What's next

The Venue is Kadam's next chapter: beyond private events, he plans rotating weekly events with different foods and décor for every holiday. The Sunday brunch — live carving station, made-to-order omelets, dessert bar — aims to bring the Orlando-resort buffet experience to Lake County "without the premium price tag or the I-4 commute," the Daily Commercial reported. After 12 years, the formula hasn't changed: "I really want to stay very competitive with fresh and new ideas to maintain our success for many years to come."
nri_angle: Master Chef Uday Kadam's journey from a village near Mumbai to Disney to Central Florida — and his restaurant's role as a community gathering place — shows how Indian restaurateurs have become cultural anchors in American suburbs.
author: Diaspora Desk
